items.stem:
The pulsed treatment produced more moth visits than darkness, even though its plants formed slightly fewer seed capsules. Continuous light reduced visits relative to darkness, with the reduction larger under bright than under dim illumination. Because plots differed only in lighting schedule, the researchers attributed the observed differences primarily to the timing and intensity of illumination.

Which comparison most strongly supports the conclusion that the intensity of continuous illumination, rather than merely its being continuous, affected the results?
choices: The dim-continuous plots had fewer moth visits than the no-light plots but still produced more visits than the bright-continuous plots.
The dim-pulsed plots had more moth visits than the dim-continuous plots, although both received dim light.
The bright-continuous plots had fewer moth visits and seed capsules than the no-light plots.
The bright-continuous plots had fewer moth visits than the dim-continuous plots, although both received continuous light.
items.stimulus: To test whether artificial light disrupts moth pollination, researchers placed identical evening-primrose plots under one of four nighttime lighting schedules. All plots contained the same number of plants and were located in the same meadow, but each plot received either no light, dim light in 15-minute pulses, dim continuous light, or bright continuous light. The researchers predicted that any artificial light would reduce both moth visits and the production of seed capsules. Figure 1 summarizes the mean results for each treatment.
items.explanation: The dim-continuous and bright-continuous treatments both used continuous illumination, so comparing them isolates intensity. The bright-continuous plots had 5.0 moth visits per flower per night, compared with 9.0 for the dim-continuous plots, supporting an effect of intensity rather than merely continuity.

per_choice.correct: The dim-continuous and bright-continuous treatments both used continuous illumination, so comparing them isolates intensity. The bright-continuous plots had 5.0 moth visits per flower per night, compared with 9.0 for the dim-continuous plots, supporting an effect of intensity rather than merely continuity.
per_choice.trap: Choice B compares dim continuous light with no light, so it changes both the presence and intensity of light. Choice C compares different schedules, not intensity, and Choice D compares bright continuous light with darkness, which also changes whether light is present.

items.stem:
The team expected mild drought to improve survival, but they also considered a simpler explanation: smaller seedlings might lose water more slowly, appearing more resilient without having been physiologically primed. The nutrient-restricted seedlings were included because they could become similarly small without experiencing water shortage. Although the mild-drought group was nearly the same size as the nutrient-restricted group at the start of severe drought, its survival was substantially higher and its root-to-shoot ratio was much larger. The researchers therefore associated the survival advantage with altered allocation to roots, while cautioning that the treatment reduced final leaf area, an important measure of growth.

Compared with the seedlings that received reduced nutrients, which statement accurately describes the mild-drought group?
choices: Its survival increased by 13 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio increased by 0.39.
Its survival increased by 13 percent, while its root-to-shoot ratio increased by 0.39.
Its survival increased by 13 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio decreased by 0.39.
Its survival increased by 3 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio increased by 0.39.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a brief water shortage could prepare seedlings to survive a later, more severe drought. They divided otherwise identical seedlings into three groups: one received no pretreatment, one experienced mild drought, and one received reduced nutrients for the same period. After a recovery period in identical conditions, all three groups underwent seven days of severe drought. Figure 1 reports each group's height at the beginning of that drought, its survival rate afterward, its final leaf area, and its root-to-shoot mass ratio.
items.explanation: The mild-drought group had a survival rate of 74%, compared with 61% for the reduced-nutrients group, an increase of 13 percentage points. Its root-to-shoot ratio was 1.12 rather than 0.73, an increase of 0.39.

per_choice.correct: The mild-drought group had a survival rate of 74%, compared with 61% for the reduced-nutrients group, an increase of 13 percentage points. Its root-to-shoot ratio was 1.12 rather than 0.73, an increase of 0.39.
per_choice.trap: Choice B confuses a percentage-point difference with a percent difference. Choice C reverses the direction of the root-to-shoot change. Choice D uses the difference between the mild-drought group’s and the untreated group’s survival rates instead of comparing the two groups named in the question.

items.stem: Which statement is best supported by both the passage and Figure 1?
choices: The bare, dark roof produced fewer pollinator visits than every other roof design.
The reflective membrane produced the greatest surface-temperature reduction, while the mixed garden produced the most pollinator visits.
The mixed garden produced the greatest surface-temperature reduction and the most pollinator visits.
The sedum roof produced the greatest surface-temperature reduction among the planted roofs and the most pollinator visits overall.
items.stimulus:
City planners studying urban heat compared four rooftop designs installed on buildings of similar height and area. Each roof was monitored during July, and researchers recorded its average midday surface temperature relative to a bare, dark roof as well as the number of pollinator visits observed each week. The reflective membrane consisted of a pale, nonliving material, while the other two experimental roofs contained plants. The sedum roof was covered by one low-growing species, whereas the mixed garden contained several flowering species of different heights. The results appear in Figure 1.

The reflective membrane produced the greatest reduction in surface temperature, but it did not provide the most pollinator activity. The planted roofs attracted more pollinators than either nonplanted roof, although the mixed garden, which attracted the most pollinators, reduced surface temperature less than the sedum roof. Because the measurements represent averages from one month, the researchers describe the results as evidence of different strengths rather than proof that one design is best for every building.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows that the reflective membrane reduced temperature by 8°C, the largest reduction, while the mixed garden received 64 weekly pollinator visits, the largest number. The passage states these same comparisons directly.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows that the reflective membrane reduced temperature by 8°C, the largest reduction, while the mixed garden received 64 weekly pollinator visits, the largest number. The passage states these same comparisons directly.
per_choice.trap: Choice C combines the mixed garden's correct pollinator result with the incorrect claim that it had the greatest cooling effect; choice D confuses the sedum roof's stronger cooling among planted roofs with the strongest cooling overall; choice A reverses the data because the bare roof received 12 visits, more than the reflective membrane's 10.

items.stem: If a city required a rooftop design to attract at least 30 weekly pollinator visits and then selected the qualifying design with the greatest temperature reduction, which design would meet those requirements?
choices: Reflective membrane
Sedum roof
Mixed garden
Bare, dark roof
items.stimulus:
City planners studying urban heat compared four rooftop designs installed on buildings of similar height and area. Each roof was monitored during July, and researchers recorded its average midday surface temperature relative to a bare, dark roof as well as the number of pollinator visits observed each week. The reflective membrane consisted of a pale, nonliving material, while the other two experimental roofs contained plants. The sedum roof was covered by one low-growing species, whereas the mixed garden contained several flowering species of different heights. The results appear in Figure 1.

The reflective membrane produced the greatest reduction in surface temperature, but it did not provide the most pollinator activity. The planted roofs attracted more pollinators than either nonplanted roof, although the mixed garden, which attracted the most pollinators, reduced surface temperature less than the sedum roof. Because the measurements represent averages from one month, the researchers describe the results as evidence of different strengths rather than proof that one design is best for every building.
items.explanation: The sedum roof attracted 38 weekly visits and reduced surface temperature by 5°C. The mixed garden also met the pollinator requirement with 64 visits, but its temperature reduction was only 4°C, so the sedum roof had the greater cooling effect among the qualifying designs.

per_choice.correct: The sedum roof attracted 38 weekly visits and reduced surface temperature by 5°C. The mixed garden also met the pollinator requirement with 64 visits, but its temperature reduction was only 4°C, so the sedum roof had the greater cooling effect among the qualifying designs.
per_choice.trap: Choice C is attractive because the mixed garden had the highest pollinator count, but the question asks for the greatest temperature reduction among designs meeting the minimum. Choice A fails the 30-visit requirement, and choice D fails both the visit requirement and the cooling comparison.

items.stem: Which conclusion about the relationship between cooling and pollinator activity is most directly supported by Figure 1?
choices: Only roofs with the greatest cooling effect can support substantial pollinator activity.
A design can attract more pollinators without producing the greatest reduction in surface temperature.
The two measures show no differences among the four roof designs.
As a roof's cooling effect increases, its pollinator activity always increases as well.
items.stimulus:
City planners studying urban heat compared four rooftop designs installed on buildings of similar height and area. Each roof was monitored during July, and researchers recorded its average midday surface temperature relative to a bare, dark roof as well as the number of pollinator visits observed each week. The reflective membrane consisted of a pale, nonliving material, while the other two experimental roofs contained plants. The sedum roof was covered by one low-growing species, whereas the mixed garden contained several flowering species of different heights. The results appear in Figure 1.

The planted roofs attracted more pollinators than either nonplanted roof, although the mixed garden, which attracted the most pollinators, reduced surface temperature less than the sedum roof. items.explanation: The mixed garden attracted the most pollinators, with 64 visits, but reduced temperature by only 4°C; the reflective membrane reduced temperature by 8°C but attracted only 10 visits. Thus, the data show that greater pollinator activity does not require the greatest cooling effect.

per_choice.correct: The mixed garden attracted the most pollinators, with 64 visits, but reduced temperature by only 4°C; the reflective membrane reduced temperature by 8°C but attracted only 10 visits. Thus, the data show that greater pollinator activity does not require the greatest cooling effect.
per_choice.trap: Choice D treats the data as a steadily increasing pattern, even though the reflective membrane and mixed garden move in opposite directions. Choice C ignores the clear numerical differences, and choice A overstates the data because the sedum and mixed garden had substantial pollinator activity despite not having the greatest cooling effect.

items.stem: Which statement most accurately incorporates the researchers' caution about the results?
choices: The results identify different advantages among the designs, but the one-month averages do not establish that a single design is universally best.
The results suggest that the reflective membrane is preferable in every situation because it cooled the most.
The results cannot be used to compare the designs because average measurements are never informative.
The results prove that mixed gardens are the best rooftop design for all buildings.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: A researcher claims that stone strips should be considered the best treatment for seedling establishment in dry conditions because they produced the most infiltration. Which evaluation of that claim is most accurate?
choices: It is supported for infiltration, but not for establishment, since stone strips had the most infiltration yet fewer seedlings than either other treatment in the dry year.
It is contradicted only in the wet year, when living crust first surpassed stone strips in seedling production.
It cannot be evaluated because the figure gives averages rather than measurements from every individual plot.
It is supported because stone strips had both the greatest infiltration and more seedlings than bare soil in the dry year.
items.stimulus:
In a semiarid grassland, researchers tested whether increasing water infiltration would improve the establishment of native seedlings. They compared plots of bare soil, plots crossed by loose-stone strips, and plots inoculated with living biological soil crust. The team measured the water that entered each plot after storms and counted seedlings during a dry year and a wet year. Because stone strips can channel water rather than distribute it evenly, the researchers warned that infiltration alone might not predict seedling establishment. The figure reports mean values across several plots at three study sites.

Although stone strips produced the greatest infiltration in both years, living-crust plots produced the greatest number of seedlings in both years. All three treatments had more seedlings in the wet year, but the size of that increase differed among treatments. The researchers therefore treated infiltration as one possible contributor to establishment rather than as a complete explanation of it.
items.explanation: The claim concerns seedling establishment, not infiltration alone. In the dry year, stone strips did have the highest infiltration, 31 mm, but they had only 28 seedlings per square meter, compared with 42 for bare soil and 57 for living crust. Therefore, the infiltration portion of the reasoning is supported, but the conclusion that stones are best for establishment is not.

per_choice.correct: The claim concerns seedling establishment, not infiltration alone. In the dry year, stone strips did have the highest infiltration, 31 mm, but they had only 28 seedlings per square meter, compared with 42 for bare soil and 57 for living crust. Therefore, the infiltration portion of the reasoning is supported, but the conclusion that stones are best for establishment is not.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the difference among treatments in the change from the dry year to the wet year?
choices: Stone-strip plots showed the largest numerical increase because their infiltration also increased the most between years.
All three treatments increased by the same number of seedlings, so the wetter conditions affected only infiltration, not the treatment differences.
Living-crust plots showed the largest numerical increase because they had the highest seedling count in each year.
Bare-soil plots showed the largest numerical increase in seedlings, even though living-crust plots remained highest in both years.
items.stimulus:
In a semiarid grassland, researchers tested whether increasing water infiltration would improve the establishment of native seedlings. They compared plots of bare soil, plots crossed by loose-stone strips, and plots inoculated with living biological soil crust. The team measured the water that entered each plot after storms and counted seedlings during a dry year and a wet year. Because stone strips can channel water rather than distribute it evenly, the researchers warned that infiltration alone might not predict seedling establishment. The figure reports mean values across several plots at three study sites.

Although stone strips produced the greatest infiltration in both years, living-crust plots produced the greatest number of seedlings in both years. All three treatments had more seedlings in the wet year, but the size of that increase differed among treatments. The researchers therefore treated infiltration as one possible contributor to establishment rather than as a complete explanation of it.
items.explanation: Seedlings increased from 42 to 68 in bare soil, a gain of 26; from 28 to 51 in stone strips, a gain of 23; and from 57 to 74 in living crust, a gain of 17. Thus, bare soil had the largest numerical increase, while living crust still had the highest count in both years.

per_choice.correct: Seedlings increased from 42 to 68 in bare soil, a gain of 26; from 28 to 51 in stone strips, a gain of 23; and from 57 to 74 in living crust, a gain of 17. Thus, bare soil had the largest numerical increase, while living crust still had the highest count in both years.
per_choice.trap: Choice C confuses having the highest count with having the largest increase. Choice A confuses the infiltration change with the seedling change, and D overlooks the different gains shown in the table.

items.stem: The researchers suggest that living crust may affect seedling establishment through more than infiltration. Which additional inference from Figure 1 most directly supports that suggestion?
choices: Stone strips had greater infiltration than bare soil in both years.
Living crust had fewer millimeters of infiltration than stone strips but more seedlings in both the dry and wet years.
Living crust had more seedlings in the wet year than in the dry year.
Bare soil had fewer millimeters of infiltration in the dry year than in the wet year.
items.stimulus:
In a semiarid grassland, researchers tested whether increasing water infiltration would improve the establishment of native seedlings. They compared plots of bare soil, plots crossed by loose-stone strips, and plots inoculated with living biological soil crust. The team measured the water that entered each plot after storms and counted seedlings during a dry year and a wet year. Because stone strips can channel water rather than distribute it evenly, the researchers warned that infiltration alone might not predict seedling establishment. The figure reports mean values across several plots at three study sites.

Although stone strips produced the greatest infiltration in both years, living-crust plots produced the greatest number of seedlings in both years. All three treatments had more seedlings in the wet year, but the size of that increase differed among treatments. The researchers therefore treated infiltration as one possible contributor to establishment rather than as a complete explanation of it.
items.explanation: Living crust recorded 26 mm of infiltration versus 31 mm for stone strips in the dry year, yet produced 57 versus 28 seedlings; in the wet year, it recorded 60 mm versus 62 mm but produced 74 versus 51 seedlings. Because crust produced more seedlings despite slightly less infiltration than stones in both years, the data support the possibility that another crust-related factor contributes to establishment.

per_choice.correct: Living crust recorded 26 mm of infiltration versus 31 mm for stone strips in the dry year, yet produced 57 versus 28 seedlings; in the wet year, it recorded 60 mm versus 62 mm but produced 74 versus 51 seedlings. Because crust produced more seedlings despite slightly less infiltration than stones in both years, the data support the possibility that another crust-related factor contributes to establishment.
per_choice.trap: Choice C is true but merely shows that wetter conditions increased seedlings. Choices A and D are also true comparisons, but neither compares a treatment's infiltration advantage or disadvantage with its seedling outcome in the way needed to support the researchers' interpretation.

items.stem: Which comparison most strongly supports the conclusion that the schedule of illumination, rather than merely the presence of light, affected the results?
choices: The dim-pulsed plots had more moth visits than the no-light plots but produced slightly fewer seed capsules.
The dim-continuous plots had fewer moth visits and fewer seed capsules than the no-light plots.
The dim-pulsed plots had more moth visits than the dim-continuous plots, although both received dim light.
The bright-continuous plots had the fewest moth visits and the fewest seed capsules of all four treatments.
items.stimulus:
To test whether artificial light disrupts moth pollination, researchers placed identical evening-primrose plots under one of four nighttime lighting schedules. All plots contained the same number of plants and were located in the same meadow, but each plot received either no light, dim light in 15-minute pulses, dim continuous light, or bright continuous light. The researchers predicted that any artificial light would reduce both moth visits and the production of seed capsules. Figure 1 summarizes the mean results for each treatment.

The pulsed treatment produced more moth visits than darkness, even though its plants formed slightly fewer seed capsules. Continuous light reduced visits relative to darkness, with the reduction larger under bright than under dim illumination. Because plots differed only in lighting schedule, the researchers attributed the observed differences primarily to the timing and intensity of illumination.
items.explanation: The dim-pulsed and dim-continuous plots both received dim light, so their different outcomes isolate the schedule: pulsed light produced 15.0 visits, whereas continuous light produced 9.0. The passage therefore supports an effect of timing, not just light's presence.

items.stem: What inference about the relationship between moth visits and seed-capsule production is best supported by the figure?
choices: Seed-capsule production is determined primarily by whether the light is bright rather than dim.
Seed-capsule production always decreases by the same proportion as moth visits.
The number of moth visits alone cannot fully account for seed-capsule production.
Moth visits have no meaningful relationship to seed-capsule production.
items.stimulus:
To test whether artificial light disrupts moth pollination, researchers placed identical evening-primrose plots under one of four nighttime lighting schedules. All plots contained the same number of plants and were located in the same meadow, but each plot received either no light, dim light in 15-minute pulses, dim continuous light, or bright continuous light. The researchers predicted that any artificial light would reduce both moth visits and the production of seed capsules. Figure 1 summarizes the mean results for each treatment.

The pulsed treatment produced more moth visits than darkness, even though its plants formed slightly fewer seed capsules. Continuous light reduced visits relative to darkness, with the reduction larger under bright than under dim illumination. Because plots differed only in lighting schedule, the researchers attributed the observed differences primarily to the timing and intensity of illumination.
items.explanation: The pulsed-light plots received the most visits, 15.0, but produced fewer seed capsules, 8.0, than the dark plots, which received 12.0 visits and produced 8.4 capsules. Thus visit count alone cannot explain the seed results. The figure does not establish that the relationship is absent, perfectly proportional, or controlled primarily by brightness.

Thus visit count alone cannot explain the seed results. The figure does not establish that the relationship is absent, perfectly proportional, or controlled primarily by brightness.
per_choice.trap: Choice B invents a constant proportional relationship not shown by the two measures. Choice D overstates the finding: the measures generally decline together under continuous light. Choice A ignores the difference between pulsed and continuous dim light and the fact that the figure reports intensity and schedule together.

Seed-capsule production was lower under dim pulsed light than under no light.
Bright continuous light produced 5.0 visits per flower, fewer than the 12.0 visits in darkness.
Dim continuous light produced 9.0 visits per flower, fewer than the 12.0 visits in darkness.

To test whether artificial light disrupts moth pollination, researchers placed identical evening-primrose plots under one of four nighttime lighting schedules. The pulsed treatment produced more moth visits than darkness, even though its plants formed slightly fewer seed capsules. Continuous light reduced visits relative to darkness, with the reduction larger under bright than under dim illumination. Because plots differed only in lighting schedule, the researchers attributed the observed differences primarily to the timing and intensity of illumination.

Dim pulsed light was the one artificial-light condition that did not reduce visits; it increased them from 12.0 in darkness to 15.0. items.stem: According to Figure 1, which map format was used by visitors who had an 81% route-completion rate?
choices: A map showing the entire museum at once
The folded paper map
The wall diagram
The touchscreen map
items.stimulus:
In 2024, researchers tested whether the format of a museum map affected visitors' ability to find several exhibits. The team recruited 180 visitors and gave each person one of three maps: a folded paper map, a touchscreen map, or a wall diagram. The visitors did not know that the map format was the focus of the study.

Each visitor used the assigned map to find four exhibits in the museum. Researchers recorded whether the visitor completed the route and how long the route took. Figure 1 shows the percentage of visitors in each group who completed the route.

The researchers noted that the touchscreen map displayed one exhibit at a time, while the other maps showed the entire museum at once. items.stem: Which statement is best supported by Figure 1 about the effect of depth on species diversity?
choices: Moving from shallow to deep water increased the mean number of species for the arched and cubical shelters but not for the slotted shelter.
Shallow water produced higher mean species counts regardless of shelter design.
Moving from shallow to deep water increased the mean number of species for every shelter design.
Depth affected the slotted shelter more strongly than it affected either of the other designs.
items.stimulus:
Marine biologists deployed three types of ceramic shelters on a reef: arched, cubical, and slotted. They wanted to know whether shelter shape affected fish species diversity, meaning the number of species using a shelter, rather than the total number of fish. To separate shelter shape from size, the researchers made every shelter with the same internal volume.

After eight weeks, the team recorded the number of fish species in each shelter and averaged the results from ten shelters at each depth. Figure 1 displays those mean counts; because each value is an average, it does not show how much individual shelters varied.

The arched design had the highest mean in deep water, while the slotted design had the highest mean in shallow water. Researchers caution that the study lasted only eight weeks, so the results do not establish which design will remain best over many seasons. Still, the contrasting results for the slotted shelter suggest that shelter shape and depth may interact rather than having separate, predictable effects.
items.explanation: The arched mean rises from 4.8 to 6.1 and the cubical mean rises from 3.9 to 5.0, while the slotted mean falls from 5.2 to 4.7. Thus, the first choice accurately describes the pattern without claiming that depth had the same effect on every design.

per_choice.correct: The arched mean rises from 4.8 to 6.1 and the cubical mean rises from 3.9 to 5.0, while the slotted mean falls from 5.2 to 4.7. Thus, the first choice accurately describes the pattern without claiming that depth had the same effect on every design.
per_choice.trap: The third choice is attractive because deep water has higher values for two designs, but it overgeneralizes by ignoring the slotted shelter's decline. The third confuses the direction of the slotted change with the size of the change, and the fourth reverses the overall pattern.

items.stem: Which shelter design shows the greatest absolute difference in its mean species count between shallow and deep water?
choices: The arched design
The cubical design
The slotted design
All three designs show the same difference
items.stimulus:
Marine biologists deployed three types of ceramic shelters on a reef: arched, cubical, and slotted. They wanted to know whether shelter shape affected fish species diversity, meaning the number of species using a shelter, rather than the total number of fish. To separate shelter shape from size, the researchers made every shelter with the same internal volume.

After eight weeks, the team recorded the number of fish species in each shelter and averaged the results from ten shelters at each depth. Figure 1 displays those mean counts; because each value is an average, it does not show how much individual shelters varied.

The arched design had the highest mean in deep water, while the slotted design had the highest mean in shallow water. Researchers caution that the study lasted only eight weeks, so the results do not establish which design will remain best over many seasons. Still, the contrasting results for the slotted shelter suggest that shelter shape and depth may interact rather than having separate, predictable effects.
items.explanation: The arched design changes by 1.3 species (6.1 minus 4.8), the cubical design by 1.1 species (5.0 minus 3.9), and the slotted design by 0.5 species (5.2 versus 4.7). Therefore, the arched design has the greatest absolute difference.

per_choice.correct: The arched design changes by 1.3 species (6.1 minus 4.8), the cubical design by 1.1 species (5.0 minus 3.9), and the slotted design by 0.5 species (5.2 versus 4.7). Therefore, the arched design has the greatest absolute difference.
per_choice.trap: The cubical choice may seem plausible because its deep-water value is exactly 5.0, but the question asks about the size of the change, not the value in deep water. The slotted choice mistakes its reversal in direction for the largest difference.

items.stem: If a manager's immediate goal is to obtain the largest mean number of fish species in shallow water, which choice is best supported by the data?
choices: Use the cubical design in shallow water.
Use the arched design in deep water instead.
Use the slotted design in shallow water.
Use the arched design in shallow water.
items.stimulus:
Marine biologists deployed three types of ceramic shelters on a reef: arched, cubical, and slotted. items.stem: Which conclusion is justified by the figure and the researchers' caution about the study's duration?
choices: The cubical design is the best general choice because its results are unaffected by depth.
The arched design should be considered permanently superior because it had the highest deep-water value.
During the eight-week trial, the arched design had the highest average across the two depths, but the study does not show that it will always be best.
The slotted design is the most reliable choice because it had the highest shallow-water value and therefore will perform best in all conditions.
items.stimulus:
Marine biologists deployed three types of ceramic shelters on a reef: arched, cubical, and slotted. They wanted to know whether shelter shape affected fish species diversity, meaning the number of species using a shelter, rather than the total number of fish. To separate shelter shape from size, the researchers made every shelter with the same internal volume.

The arched design had the highest mean in deep water, while the slotted design had the highest mean in shallow water. Researchers caution that the study lasted only eight weeks, so the results do not establish which design will remain best over many seasons. Still, the contrasting results for the slotted shelter suggest that shelter shape and depth may interact rather than having separate, predictable effects.
items.explanation: The arched design's two values total 10.9, higher than the slotted design's 9.9 and the cubical design's 8.9, so it has the highest two-depth average during this trial. However, the passage explicitly says the eight-week study cannot establish which design will remain best over many seasons.

items.stem: Compared with the seedlings that received no pretreatment, which statement accurately describes the mild-drought group?
choices: Its survival increased by 16 percent, while its final leaf area decreased by 8 square centimeters.
Its survival increased by 16 percentage points, while its final leaf area decreased by 8 square centimeters.
Its survival increased by 16 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio decreased by 0.41.
Its height at drought onset decreased by 2.8 centimeters, while its survival increased by 8 percentage points.
items.stimulus:
Researchers tested whether a brief water shortage could prepare seedlings to survive a later, more severe drought. They divided otherwise identical seedlings into three groups: one received no pretreatment, one experienced mild drought, and one received reduced nutrients for the same period. After a recovery period in identical conditions, all three groups underwent seven days of severe drought. Figure 1 reports each group's height at the beginning of that drought, its survival rate afterward, its final leaf area, and its root-to-shoot mass ratio.

The team expected mild drought to improve survival, but they also considered a simpler explanation: smaller seedlings might lose water more slowly, appearing more resilient without having been physiologically primed. The nutrient-restricted seedlings were included because they could become similarly small without experiencing water shortage. Although the mild-drought group was nearly the same size as the nutrient-restricted group at the start of severe drought, its survival was substantially higher and its root-to-shoot ratio was much larger. The researchers therefore associated the survival advantage with altered allocation to roots, while cautioning that the treatment reduced final leaf area, an important measure of growth.
items.explanation: The mild-drought group survived at a rate of 74%, compared with 58% for the untreated group, an increase of 16 percentage points. Its final leaf area was 34 cm² rather than 42 cm², a decrease of 8 cm².

per_choice.correct: The mild-drought group survived at a rate of 74%, compared with 58% for the untreated group, an increase of 16 percentage points. Its final leaf area was 34 cm² rather than 42 cm², a decrease of 8 cm².
per_choice.trap: Choice A confuses a percentage-point change with a percent change; choice C reverses the direction of the root-to-shoot change; choice D uses the height difference as though it were the survival difference.

items.trap: Choice A confuses a percentage-point change with a percent change; choice C reverses the direction of the root-to-shoot change; choice D uses the height difference as though it were the survival difference.

items.stem: Which comparison most directly supports the researchers' claim that the mild-drought group's greater survival was not caused solely by its smaller size?
choices: The no-pretreatment group versus the reduced-nutrient group, because both groups received no mild drought.
The mild-drought group versus the reduced-nutrient group, because the groups had nearly equal heights but differed greatly in survival and root-to-shoot ratio.
The no-pretreatment group versus the mild-drought group, because those groups differed in both survival and height.
The mild-drought group versus all other groups, because it had the largest root-to-shoot ratio and the smallest final leaf area.
items.stimulus:
Researchers tested whether a brief water shortage could prepare seedlings to survive a later, more severe drought. They divided otherwise identical seedlings into three groups: one received no pretreatment, one experienced mild drought, and one received reduced nutrients for the same period. After a recovery period in identical conditions, all three groups underwent seven days of severe drought. Figure 1 reports each group's height at the beginning of that drought, its survival rate afterward, its final leaf area, and its root-to-shoot mass ratio.

The team expected mild drought to improve survival, but they also considered a simpler explanation: smaller seedlings might lose water more slowly, appearing more resilient without having been physiologically primed. The nutrient-restricted seedlings were included because they could become similarly small without experiencing water shortage. Although the mild-drought group was nearly the same size as the nutrient-restricted group at the start of severe drought, its survival was substantially higher and its root-to-shoot ratio was much larger. The researchers therefore associated the survival advantage with altered allocation to roots, while cautioning that the treatment reduced final leaf area, an important measure of growth.
items.explanation: The reduced-nutrient seedlings were nearly the same height as the mild-drought seedlings at the onset of severe drought, yet their survival was 61% rather than 74% and their root-to-shoot ratio was 0.73 rather than 1.12. This comparison weakens the explanation that small size alone produced the survival advantage.

per_choice.correct: The reduced-nutrient seedlings were nearly the same height as the mild-drought seedlings at the onset of severe drought, yet their survival was 61% rather than 74% and their root-to-shoot ratio was 0.73 rather than 1.12. This comparison weakens the explanation that small size alone produced the survival advantage.
per_choice.trap: Choice C identifies a difference but cannot separate size from the effects of water pretreatment. Choice A establishes that both groups lacked mild drought but does not control for size. Choice D describes the mild-drought group's data without providing the crucial same-size comparison.

items.stem: Which conclusion most precisely captures the tradeoff shown by Figure 1?
choices: Mild drought was beneficial overall because the group with the highest survival also had the greatest final leaf area.
The untreated group performed best because its larger seedlings had both the highest leaf area and the highest survival.
Mild drought improved drought survival but was associated with less final leaf area than either comparison group.
Reduced nutrients produced an intermediate outcome for every measure, showing that growth and survival changed together.

items.explanation: The mild-drought group had the highest survival, 74%, but the smallest final leaf area, 34 cm². Thus the treatment improved one measured outcome while reducing another, so it cannot be described as uniformly beneficial.

items.stem: Why is the reduced-nutrient group especially informative when interpreting the mild-drought group's survival advantage?
choices: It shows that reduced nutrients and mild drought had identical effects on final leaf area, so their other measurements can be treated as identical as well.
It shows that the mild-drought group had the smallest seedlings, which directly proves that small size caused its higher survival.
It shows that seedlings of nearly the same initial height did not necessarily have the same survival, allowing the effects of size to be distinguished from those of pretreatment.
It shows that nutrient reduction produced the greatest root-to-shoot ratio, confirming that root allocation was unrelated to pretreatment.
items.stimulus:
Researchers tested whether a brief water shortage could prepare seedlings to survive a later, more severe drought. They divided otherwise identical seedlings into three groups: one received no pretreatment, one experienced mild drought, and one received reduced nutrients for the same period. After a recovery period in identical conditions, all three groups underwent seven days of severe drought. Figure 1 reports each group's height at the beginning of that drought, its survival rate afterward, its final leaf area, and its root-to-shoot mass ratio.

The team expected mild drought to improve survival, but they also considered a simpler explanation: smaller seedlings might lose water more slowly, appearing more resilient without having been physiologically primed. The nutrient-restricted seedlings were included because they could become similarly small without experiencing water shortage. Although the mild-drought group was nearly the same size as the nutrient-restricted group at the start of severe drought, its survival was substantially higher and its root-to-shoot ratio was much larger. The researchers therefore associated the survival advantage with altered allocation to roots, while cautioning that the treatment reduced final leaf area, an important measure of growth.
items.explanation: The two groups were almost identical in height at the start of severe drought—15.4 and 15.6 cm—but their survival rates differed substantially, 74% versus 61%. Their root-to-shoot ratios also differed greatly, which allows the researchers to consider pretreatment-related allocation rather than attributing the result only to size.

per_choice.correct: The two groups were almost identical in height at the start of severe drought—15.4 and 15.6 cm—but their survival rates differed substantially, 74% versus 61%. Their root-to-shoot ratios also differed greatly, which allows the researchers to consider pretreatment-related allocation rather than attributing the result only to size.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by considering the vegetation results in Figure 1 together with the researchers' final assessment?
choices: The deep-water treatment was the most successful overall because it produced the least invasive cover.
The three treatments produced essentially equivalent ecological outcomes because each led in at least one measured category.
The shallow-water treatment was the most successful overall because it produced the greatest number of native stems.
The seasonally variable treatment offered the most balanced results across plant competition and animal diversity, despite not leading in native stems.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows that seasonally variable water had lower invasive cover than shallow water and the highest number of dragonfly species, while the final sentence explicitly calls it a compromise even though it produced fewer native stems than shallow water.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows that seasonally variable water had lower invasive cover than shallow water and the highest number of dragonfly species, while the final sentence explicitly calls it a compromise even though it produced fewer native stems than shallow water.
per_choice.trap: Choice C focuses only on the native-stem measure, choice A focuses only on invasive cover, and choice B mistakes having different category leaders for having equivalent overall results.

items.stem: Which finding most directly qualifies the claim that maintaining deep water suppresses invasive plants?
choices: Deep water had more native stems than shallow water, but it also had higher summer phosphate.
Deep water supported the most dragonfly species, even though it had the highest invasive cover.
Deep water had the lowest invasive cover, but it also had the fewest native stems and the lowest summer oxygen level.
Deep water had the highest summer oxygen level, although its phosphate concentration was the lowest.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: Figure 1 confirms that deep water had the least invasive cover, but it also had the fewest native stems; Figure 2 shows that it had the lowest summer dissolved oxygen. These accompanying results qualify the benefit rather than disproving it.

per_choice.trap: The other choices alter one or more rankings in the figures: shallow water had more native stems, variable water had the most dragonfly species and highest summer oxygen, and deep water did not have the highest invasive cover.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: Which treatment-and-season comparison best supports the researchers' statement that shallow water may have favored plant emergence partly because of phosphate availability?
choices: Seasonally variable water had the most dragonfly species in Figure 1 and the highest summer oxygen reading in Figure 2.
Shallow water had the highest spring oxygen reading in Figure 2 and more native stems than deep water in Figure 1.
Shallow water had the most native stems in Figure 1 and the highest phosphate reading in summer in Figure 2.
Deep water had the least invasive cover in Figure 1 and the lowest phosphate reading in both seasons in Figure 2.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: The proposed explanation concerns both plant emergence and phosphate availability. Shallow water led in native stems and had the highest summer phosphate concentration, the specific combination the researchers identify as potentially relevant.

per_choice.correct: The proposed explanation concerns both plant emergence and phosphate availability. Shallow water led in native stems and had the highest summer phosphate concentration, the specific combination the researchers identify as potentially relevant.
per_choice.trap: Choice A accurately combines two results but concerns dragonflies and oxygen, not plant emergence and phosphate; C concerns suppression of invasives; D combines true facts but does not connect the native-stem advantage with the highest phosphate level.

items.stem: What does the comparison of spring and summer phosphate readings indicate about the shallow-water treatment that is not true of either of the other treatments?
choices: Its phosphate concentration increased rather than decreased, while phosphate declined in both the seasonally variable and deep-water treatments.
It had the lowest phosphate concentration in both seasons, although its native-stem count was highest.
Its phosphate concentration remained constant, while phosphate increased in both the seasonally variable and deep-water treatments.
It had the largest phosphate decrease and the lowest summer dissolved oxygen level.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: Choice A is correct because the shallow-water treatment was the only one whose phosphate concentration increased from spring to summer. Phosphate decreased in both the seasonally variable and deep-water treatments.

per_choice.correct: Choice A is correct because the shallow-water treatment was the only one whose phosphate concentration increased from spring to summer. Phosphate decreased in both the seasonally variable and deep-water treatments.
per_choice.trap: Choice D confuses the treatments’ oxygen results with their phosphate changes: the passage identifies deep water as having limited oxygen, but it does not say shallow water had the largest phosphate decrease or the lowest summer oxygen.

items.stem: Which statement most accurately reconciles the seasonally variable plots' lower native-stem count with the researchers' favorable assessment of that treatment?
choices: Their lower stem count was offset by their having the highest phosphate concentration in both seasons and the most native stems.
Their lower stem count was offset by their having the highest invasive cover and the lowest summer oxygen level.
Their lower stem count was offset by their producing more native stems than shallow water but fewer invasive plants than deep water.
Their lower stem count was offset by the lowest invasive cover among the two treatments with more than 20 native stems and by the greatest dragonfly diversity.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: Seasonally variable plots had 26 native stems, fewer than shallow plots, but only 9% invasive cover and 7 dragonfly species. The phrase 'among the two treatments with more than 20 native stems' accurately distinguishes its invasive-cover advantage from the deep treatment's lower cover.

per_choice.correct: Seasonally variable plots had 26 native stems, fewer than shallow plots, but only 9% invasive cover and 7 dragonfly species. The phrase 'among the two treatments with more than 20 native stems' accurately distinguishes its invasive-cover advantage from the deep treatment's lower cover.
per_choice.trap: Choice B reverses the oxygen and invasive-cover rankings; C attributes shallow water's phosphate and stem advantages to variable water; D reverses both native-stem comparisons.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: Which pair of results most clearly illustrates the researchers' warning that water depth altered several conditions at once rather than producing a single uniform effect?
choices: As the treatment shifted from shallow to deep water, invasive cover fell while native-stem abundance also fell.
As the treatment shifted from shallow to deep water, dragonfly diversity rose while summer oxygen also rose.
As the treatment shifted from shallow to deep water, phosphate fell while native-stem abundance rose.
As the treatment shifted from shallow to deep water, invasive cover rose while phosphate fell.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: The figures show a tradeoff: deep water reduced invasive cover from 18% to 6% but also reduced native stems from 31 to 17. That opposing movement across measures illustrates why no treatment was best on every outcome.

per_choice.correct: The figures show a tradeoff: deep water reduced invasive cover from 18% to 6% but also reduced native stems from 31 to 17. That opposing movement across measures illustrates why no treatment was best on every outcome.
per_choice.trap: Choice B reverses the dragonfly and summer-oxygen trends; C reverses the native-stem trend; D reverses the invasive-cover trend, even though phosphate does decline.

items.stem: If a restoration manager's stated goal were to maximize native stems while avoiding the treatment with the greatest invasive cover, which treatment would the figures support choosing?
choices: Shallow water, because it maximized native stems even though it also maximized invasive cover.
Deep water, because it minimized invasive cover even though it also minimized native stems and summer oxygen.
No treatment, because the figures show that every treatment had the same invasive-cover percentage.
Seasonally variable water, because it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but avoided shallow water's highest invasive-cover value.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists studying the restoration of abandoned cranberry bogs asked how water-level management affects the return of native wetland plants. They divided 18 similar plots among three treatments: shallow water maintained year-round, water levels allowed to rise and fall seasonally, and deep water maintained year-round. After two growing seasons, they counted native stems and estimated the percentage of ground covered by invasive plants. Figure 1 reports the treatment means.

The shallow plots produced the most native stems, but they also had the greatest invasive cover, whereas the seasonally variable plots supported the most dragonfly species. To interpret these differences, the researchers measured dissolved oxygen and phosphate in each treatment during spring and summer. Figure 2 gives the average readings, in milligrams per liter.

The researchers caution that water depth did not produce a single winner on every measure because it altered several conditions at once. Shallow water favored plant emergence, perhaps in part because its relatively high phosphate concentration persisted into summer, while deep water limited both phosphate and oxygen. They therefore describe seasonal variation as a compromise: it produced fewer native stems than shallow water but substantially less invasive cover, the highest dragonfly diversity, and the highest summer oxygen level.
items.explanation: The goal requires balancing two conditions rather than maximizing one. Shallow water has the most stems but also the greatest invasive cover; deep water avoids invasive cover but has the fewest stems; seasonally variable water has 26 stems and avoids the maximum invasive-cover result.

per_choice.correct: The goal requires balancing two conditions rather than maximizing one. Shallow water has the most stems but also the greatest invasive cover; deep water avoids invasive cover but has the fewest stems; seasonally variable water has 26 stems and avoids the maximum invasive-cover result.
per_choice.trap: Choice A ignores the stated avoidance condition, choice B gives priority to minimizing invasives rather than maximizing stems, and choice C contradicts Figure 1's distinct percentages.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, which finding most directly challenges the researchers' prediction about combining treatments?
choices: The combined treatment recorded the same number of flower species as the spring-burn treatment but fewer bee visits and a lower seed-production rate.
The spring-burn treatment produced a higher seed-production rate than the unmowed treatment and the mowing-alone treatment.
Mowing alone produced more flower species than the unmowed treatment and more bee visits than the unmowed treatment.
The unmowed treatment attracted more flies than bees, whereas the mowing-alone treatment attracted more bees than flies.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists investigated whether different management treatments changed both the variety of flowers and the insects that visited a restored prairie. They established thirty-two plots with similar soil and divided them among four treatments: no mowing, mowing alone, a spring burn, and a spring burn followed by late-season mowing. Each treatment was assigned to eight plots, and researchers recorded flower species, insect visits, and the percentage of flowers producing seeds during two summers. Because the plots were close together, the researchers treated the study as a comparison of management regimes rather than of separate prairies.

Researchers had predicted that combining the burn with late mowing would produce the strongest results by extending the period of flowering. Instead, the spring-burn treatment alone had the highest bee-visit rate and the highest seed-production rate, while the combined treatment matched it in flower-species count but not in either of those measures. The unmowed plots, despite receiving no disturbance, attracted more flies than bees and had the lowest values for flower diversity and seed production. The researchers noted that the flower-species measure counted every species seen during the season, so it could not show whether flowers were available at the same time as peak insect activity.

This limitation may explain why equal seasonal flower counts did not produce equal bee visits in the two burned treatments. The pattern suggests that management can channel visitor traffic toward particular insect groups without simply increasing every kind of visitor. Researchers also cautioned that the figure cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed-production rates, since the treatments may have changed other features of the plots as well. They therefore described the burn treatment as the most promising regime in this trial, not as a universally superior treatment for every prairie.
items.explanation: The prediction concerned the combination producing the strongest results by extending flowering. Figure 1 shows that the combined treatment tied the burn alone in flower-species count but fell below it in bee visits and seed production, directly contradicting the prediction. The other choices report comparisons in the figure but do not specifically challenge the predicted advantage of combining treatments.

per_choice.correct: The prediction concerned the combination producing the strongest results by extending flowering. Figure 1 shows that the combined treatment tied the burn alone in flower-species count but fell below it in bee visits and seed production, directly contradicting the prediction. The other choices report comparisons in the figure but do not specifically challenge the predicted advantage of combining treatments.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is true and may seem relevant because it identifies the strongest seed-production treatment, but it does not compare the combined treatment with the burn alone, which is the crucial test of the prediction.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: Which conclusion is most strongly supported by both the passage and Figure 1, rather than by the figure alone?
choices: The spring burn was the most promising treatment in this particular trial, but the results do not establish that it will be best in every prairie.
The spring burn caused bees to produce more seeds because bees visited those plots most often.
Late mowing reduced the number of flower species available during the season.
The spring burn should replace mowing and no-mowing practices in prairie restoration.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists investigated whether different management treatments changed both the variety of flowers and the insects that visited a restored prairie. They established thirty-two plots with similar soil and divided them among four treatments: no mowing, mowing alone, a spring burn, and a spring burn followed by late-season mowing. Each treatment was assigned to eight plots, and researchers recorded flower species, insect visits, and the percentage of flowers producing seeds during two summers. Because the plots were close together, the researchers treated the study as a comparison of management regimes rather than of separate prairies.

Researchers had predicted that combining the burn with late mowing would produce the strongest results by extending the period of flowering. Instead, the spring-burn treatment alone had the highest bee-visit rate and the highest seed-production rate, while the combined treatment matched it in flower-species count but not in either of those measures. The unmowed plots, despite receiving no disturbance, attracted more flies than bees and had the lowest values for flower diversity and seed production. The researchers noted that the flower-species measure counted every species seen during the season, so it could not show whether flowers were available at the same time as peak insect activity.

This limitation may explain why equal seasonal flower counts did not produce equal bee visits in the two burned treatments. The pattern suggests that management can channel visitor traffic toward particular insect groups without simply increasing every kind of visitor. Researchers also cautioned that the figure cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed-production rates, since the treatments may have changed other features of the plots as well. They therefore described the burn treatment as the most promising regime in this trial, not as a universally superior treatment for every prairie.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows that the spring burn had the highest bee visits and seed-production rate, and the final paragraph explicitly calls it the most promising regime in this trial while rejecting a universal claim. The passage specifically says the data cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed production, does not report a reduced seasonal species count from late mowing, and does not recommend replacing all other practices.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows that the spring burn had the highest bee visits and seed-production rate, and the final paragraph explicitly calls it the most promising regime in this trial while rejecting a universal claim. The passage specifically says the data cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed production, does not report a reduced seasonal species count from late mowing, and does not recommend replacing all other practices.
per_choice.trap: Choice B converts an association into causation, exactly the inference the researchers caution against. Choice C confuses the unmeasured timing of flowers with the measured seasonal species count, and D overstates the qualified conclusion.

items.tests: Reading a figure alongside prose and judging which statement the data supports.

items.stem: The information about seasonal flower counts most directly supports which inference?
choices: The treatment with the greatest flower-species count must also have the greatest number of insect visits.
Flower species were counted only during the period when bee activity was highest.
The researchers' flower counts were too inconsistent to compare among treatments.
Two treatments can have the same total number of flower species while differing in when those flowers are available to insects.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists investigated whether different management treatments changed both the variety of flowers and the insects that visited a restored prairie. They established thirty-two plots with similar soil and divided them among four treatments: no mowing, mowing alone, a spring burn, and a spring burn followed by late-season mowing. Each treatment was assigned to eight plots, and researchers recorded flower species, insect visits, and the percentage of flowers producing seeds during two summers. Because the plots were close together, the researchers treated the study as a comparison of management regimes rather than of separate prairies.

Researchers had predicted that combining the burn with late mowing would produce the strongest results by extending the period of flowering. Instead, the spring-burn treatment alone had the highest bee-visit rate and the highest seed-production rate, while the combined treatment matched it in flower-species count but not in either of those measures. The unmowed plots, despite receiving no disturbance, attracted more flies than bees and had the lowest values for flower diversity and seed production. The researchers noted that the flower-species measure counted every species seen during the season, so it could not show whether flowers were available at the same time as peak insect activity.

This limitation may explain why equal seasonal flower counts did not produce equal bee visits in the two burned treatments. The pattern suggests that management can channel visitor traffic toward particular insect groups without simply increasing every kind of visitor. Researchers also cautioned that the figure cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed-production rates, since the treatments may have changed other features of the plots as well. They therefore described the burn treatment as the most promising regime in this trial, not as a universally superior treatment for every prairie.
items.explanation: The passage says the count included every species seen during the season and therefore could not show whether flowers were present during peak insect activity. Thus equal totals in the two burned treatments could coexist with different visitation rates. The passage does not say counts were made only at peak activity or too inconsistent to compare, and Figure 1 disproves the claim that the highest species count guarantees the most visits.

per_choice.correct: The passage says the count included every species seen during the season and therefore could not show whether flowers were present during peak insect activity. Thus equal totals in the two burned treatments could coexist with different visitation rates. The passage does not say counts were made only at peak activity or too inconsistent to compare, and Figure 1 disproves the claim that the highest species count guarantees the most visits.
per_choice.trap: Choice A follows a tempting but unsupported assumption that more flower types automatically produce more visits. The passage instead emphasizes timing as a possible reason the equal counts did not yield equal visitation.

items.stem: Which quoted sentence provides the clearest evidence for the claim that the researchers distinguish an association from a demonstrated causal relationship?
choices: 'Researchers also cautioned that the figure cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed-production rates, since the treatments may have changed other features of the plots as well.'
'The unmowed plots, despite receiving no disturbance, attracted more flies than bees and had the lowest values for flower diversity and seed production.'
'They therefore described the burn treatment as the most promising regime in this trial, not as a universally superior treatment for every prairie.'
'This limitation may explain why equal seasonal flower counts did not produce equal bee visits in the two burned treatments.'

The first reports an association, the second offers an explanation for a pattern, and the fourth limits generalization, but neither directly states the association-versus-causation distinction.

items.stem: A researcher claims, 'Because the spring-burn and combined treatments produced the same flower-species count, late mowing had no effect on the prairie.' Which response is best supported by the passage?
choices: The claim is supported because late mowing increased both bee visits and seed production relative to burning alone.
The claim is contradicted because the combined treatment produced fewer flower species than the spring-burn treatment.
The claim is supported because flower-species count is the only outcome that the researchers measured directly.
The claim is too broad because the equal seasonal species counts do not rule out effects on the timing of flowers or on insect visitation and seed production.
items.stimulus:
Ecologists investigated whether different management treatments changed both the variety of flowers and the insects that visited a restored prairie. They established thirty-two plots with similar soil and divided them among four treatments: no mowing, mowing alone, a spring burn, and a spring burn followed by late-season mowing. Each treatment was assigned to eight plots, and researchers recorded flower species, insect visits, and the percentage of flowers producing seeds during two summers. Because the plots were close together, the researchers treated the study as a comparison of management regimes rather than of separate prairies.

Researchers had predicted that combining the burn with late mowing would produce the strongest results by extending the period of flowering. Instead, the spring-burn treatment alone had the highest bee-visit rate and the highest seed-production rate, while the combined treatment matched it in flower-species count but not in either of those measures. The unmowed plots, despite receiving no disturbance, attracted more flies than bees and had the lowest values for flower diversity and seed production. The researchers noted that the flower-species measure counted every species seen during the season, so it could not show whether flowers were available at the same time as peak insect activity.

This limitation may explain why equal seasonal flower counts did not produce equal bee visits in the two burned treatments. The pattern suggests that management can channel visitor traffic toward particular insect groups without simply increasing every kind of visitor. Researchers also cautioned that the figure cannot establish that bees caused the higher seed-production rates, since the treatments may have changed other features of the plots as well. They therefore described the burn treatment as the most promising regime in this trial, not as a universally superior treatment for every prairie.
items.explanation: The two treatments both recorded 15 flower species, but the combined treatment had fewer bee visits and a lower seed-production rate, and the passage says seasonal counts cannot reveal timing. Therefore equal species totals cannot justify the broad claim that late mowing had no effect.

per_choice.correct: The two treatments both recorded 15 flower species, but the combined treatment had fewer bee visits and a lower seed-production rate, and the passage says seasonal counts cannot reveal timing. Therefore equal species totals cannot justify the broad claim that late mowing had no effect.
per_choice.trap: Choice B misreads the figure: the treatments tied at 15 species. Choice A reverses the figure, while B ignores the other outcomes that were measured directly.
